extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, literary critics, and psychoanalytic readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting theoretical criteria that distinguish wit from the comic and the techniques that produce each (e.g., unmasking, nonsense-wit, imitation, comparison), with conditions that enable comic pleasure to arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmasking (mechanism of comic-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic process that degrades dignity by calling attention to a common human frailty or the dependence of mental functions upon physical needs; it uncovers psychic automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: marriage-agent anecdotes that reveal the agent's automatism; stories where a cry or act 'unmasks' someone admired as merely human. Unmasking can serve as a 'facade' for wit (the anecdote may be comic on the surface but 'a splendidly put together piece of wit' for those who see the hidden meaning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through a trifle / through the opposite (technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical means of producing wit or comic effect by representing something significant with a trivial sign or by expressing a thought through its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using a trivial cry to indicate the point (representation through a trifle); an agent trying to prove people are rich by thereby proving they are poor (expression through the opposite). These techniques can make a story serve both as comic and as wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit reopens hidden sources of comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit functions to reopen hidden sources of comic pleasure; any clever evocation of the comic may in looser analogy be called a witticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud notes that usage of speech does not enter scientifically into the nature of wit as evolved here, so artifice that brings to light barefaced comic may be called witticism in looser usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense-wit / giving free play to unconscious (faulty) thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique where wit gives free play to modes of thinking common in the unconscious (so-called 'faulty thinking'), producing witticisms that may appear as nonsense and may fuse wit and comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These produce wit by forming compromises between the rational critic and impulse to word-pleasure; when foreconscious thought is left to unconscious elaboration, the result can appear as nonsense to the critic but still convey meaning through the hearer's unconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unconscious 'faulty thinking' as a technical resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit utilizes forms of thinking that are common in the unconscious (e.g., juxtapositions, condensations) though they are forbidden in conscious thought; these modes can provoke little opposition if disguised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If faulty thinking is disguised (e.g., by a semblance of logic), it may avoid critic's protest; undesguised faulty thinking will provoke contradiction. Example techniques: condensations, slips, fusions that mimic dream-work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguising faulty thinking with a semblance of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategy of wit: invest faulty/unconscious thinking with a veneer of logic to avoid the critic's protest and maintain witty effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: stories that smuggle absurd or 'faulty' reasoning into a superficially logical form (fancy cake and liqueur, salmon with mayonnaise). If the disguise fails, the critic will protest and wit may be lost or appear merely comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual neutralization / juxtaposition of well-motivated thoughts (comic via unconscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect through the unconscious operation where several well-motivated thoughts neutralize one another when placed together, yielding absurdity (a characteristic of unconscious thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the borrowed kettle returned with a hole — owner excuses: (1) he didn't borrow it, (2) it had a hole already, (3) he returned it intact. Each motive is plausible but together produce comic absurdity. Analogous to dream-work where incompatible thoughts sit side-by-side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference of expenditure (comparison of two expenditures) as source of comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal source of comic pleasure: comparison between two psychic expenditures (what is expended in expectation/understanding vs what is actually required), where a surplus (superfluous expenditure) is discharged as comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud repeatedly emphasizes tracing comic pleasure to a 'comparison of two expenditures' rather than other contrasts. This principle explains many comic forms (unmasking, imitation, faulty thinking) by quantifying expectation vs required mental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychic localization: wit in the unconscious vs comic in the foreconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is localized in the sphere of the unconscious (it arises from unconscious mechanisms), whereas the comic's source is not similarly localized and is adjudged to the foreconscious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction helps separate wit from comic: wit contributes from unconscious word-pleasure sources; comic pleasure is observable as a discharge in foreconscious comparison of expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of imitation (degradation toward the mechanical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation produces comic pleasure when human behavior or expression reminds us of a machine (degradation of human to inanimate/mechanical), reducing required expenditure and releasing pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's view is cited: 'the attitudes, gestures, and movements of the human body are laughable in exact proportion as that body reminds us of a mere machine.' Freud reframes this as a reduction in expenditure due to repetition or perfect agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinence of comparison (quality required for comic comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good comparison must be pertinent — it should genuinely call attention to an existing agreement between two different objects; only pertinent comparisons can produce comic effects when they create a disparity of abstraction expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing the less familiar to the more familiar helps intellectual work; comic emerges when comparing something serious/intellectual/sublime to something banal/lowly causing degradation and discharge of expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic via degradation in comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic arises in comparison when a strange/abstract/serious thing is aligned with a banal/lowly object, causing degradation of the lofty item and yielding comic pleasure from the drop in required abstraction expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comparing Truth to a torch that singes people's beards (wit when not degraded; comic when degradation dominates). The comic of comparison is a concrete case of degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit techniques: double meaning, allusion, unification (forcing two views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit often forces the hearer to hold two different views simultaneously (double meaning, allusion, unification), producing intellectual pleasure; wit thereby may avoid comic appearance by evading absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: double meaning, allusive lines (Heine's 'buttons tore from the pants of my patience'), and unifications like Nestroy's 'memory as a warehouse' which are both witty and (sometimes) comical depending on degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense-wit vs comic-nonsense distinction (Janus-faced requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: True wit often presents a double face: one view sees nonsense of wording, the other (via unconscious suggestion) finds sense. When one of these faces is absent (stunted wit), the production tends toward comic nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wippchen examples: condensations and substitutions that produce only nonsense-view (one face empty) are 'stunted' wit and typically produce comic effect rather than genuine wit; whether to call them 'bad wit' or not is subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of inadequacy (absolute insufficiency compared to an expected form)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a riddle, verse, or form utterly fails to meet essential conditions of its genre (absolute insufficiency), this inadequacy can be irresistibly comic — the failure compared to expectations creates discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a riddle whose answer is perfectly ordinary but defended by absurd displacements (herring/towel exchange) — its foolish insufficiency makes it comic. The same mechanism applies to inept poetry (Kempner) where intentions and clumsiness combine to produce laughter rather than anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitable comic vs accidental (situational) comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish cases where the comic appears 'regularly and as if necessarily' (inevitable comic) from those where comic effect depends on conditions or observer viewpoint (accidental comic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud suggests creating two classes and then examining conditions essential to each; there will nonetheless be exceptions to inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of isolation of the comic — (a) happy disposition / 'in the mood for laughing'
rubrics_metrics.description: A favorable general disposition (euphoria) makes many things seem comic because comparison to the normal expenditure yields discharge; being 'in the mood' amplifies comic potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one is predisposed to laugh, small differences are sufficient; this mood is itself what wit/comic methods attempt to regain from single points if euphoria is absent generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of isolation — (b) expectation/premeditation of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person expects comic entertainment or deliberately puts themselves in a comic frame of mind, even slight differences produce comic effect (audience willing to laugh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attending a comic lecture or theater primes one to laugh at things that would not be comic in everyday life; people may later be ashamed of laughing at things they wouldn't normally find funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of isolation — (c) unfavorable mental occupations reduce comic discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious imaginative or abstract mental activity consumes investing energies, making it harder for the surplus expenditure to discharge as comic pleasure; only large, unexpected differences will break through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract contemplation or tasks that suspend ideational mimicry are unfavorable to comic; comic better arises when attention is not absorbed in serious thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of isolation — (d) fixing attention on the comparison destroys comic release
rubrics_metrics.description: If attention is fixed on the comparison that could give rise to comic pleasure, the occasion for discharge vanishes and the comic force is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A movement or mental act loses its comic quality when the observer scrutinizes the comparison; premeditated analysis can prevent the discharge that produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precaution: avoid reutilizing the superfluous expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: For comic pleasure to occur, recognized superfluous expenditure must not be put to other use; if the surplus energy is re-utilized, comic discharge (laughter) cannot follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both wit and comic must guard against transforming the recognized surplus into some other purposeful use; this is why certain formal precautions are necessary in constructing wit or comic effects.
